items.title: A Best-Selling Author Shares the Real Reason to Write (And a Secret to Keep Doing It)
items.label: Blogs
items.excerpt:
🫧 Open on Bubbles

Unboxing the first copies of your book feels like opening Christmas presents.

It’s the excitement of holding something that once existed only in your head and on post-it notes.

It’s the satisfaction of seeing an idea come to life after an emotional roller coaster .

In Story Telling: A Writing Life , Chilean author Isabel Allende writes,

“I once heard Elizabeth Gilbert say that we should not expect our writing to give us money or fame. We write because we love the process. I would add that we should not expect to publish either. Just do it.”

Money and fame can be rewarding.

I don’t want fame, but making a living from my words sounds appealing.

But the real reward is who you become by writing.

It’s seeing the world through a new pair of lenses.

It’s enjoying the quiet moments at the keyboard.

It’s dropping everything to write down an idea before you forget it.

Writing keeps me healthy and alive , and makes me insane.

まだ自分ごとのようには他人に説明出来ないけど、わかりやすかった！飲み込みやすいと言うんでしょうか？脳には認知共感と感情共感というものがあるっていうのもわかりやすかった！（HotとColdっていう言い方もしてました）Psychopathも全員が犯罪者じゃないぜっていう締めくくりと、脳科学、遺伝、社会学合わせて見る。そして、早めにサイコパス感を感知したら早めに手を打つと良い。Love wins的なメッセージでした。脳科学的には全人工の２%はサイコパスらしい。この計算的に、今までどこかしらでサイコパスさんと何かしら出会ったことがあるのでしょう。人に優しく、でも自分も守ろう。もしくは、人にあんまり期待しない？っていうのも自己保護なのかもしれません。色々と面白かったです。心理学に興味ある人にはオススメな本でしたー。

items.title: Silence
items.label: Small Web
items.excerpt:
And then, there is the silence. The silence when you've just finished a book.

It's a weird silence, not a silence as far as sound goes. Roadwork is still roaring by the window, the fan is still humming slowly, the dog is still munching on its kibbles. But a silence of the mind.

The characters have been jumping out the pages and into your mind, each speaking with their own voice, sharing vivid images of their lives. You are somewhere with them, listening to them, and then the last page, you close the book and there's the silence.

A silence of pondering, not really knowing what to say next. The usual voice inside your mind hasn't taken its place back, it's empty and quiet.

You are left with feelings that precede thoughts. Feelings that are part your own, part those of the book. Illusions of your life pasted onto the ones of the characters.

Feelings filled of what ifs and rememberings of what could have been and what could be.

A silence that isn't peaceful, it's a silence where you…

Round and round he goes, hustling in place. A determined entrepreneur has traded his standing desk for a human-sized hamster wheel parked in the center of the office.

The wheel spins endlessly, generating lots of motion but no forward movement.

Disability representation in pop culture is far and few between, so whenever we have any, it needs to be celebrated and scrutinized in equal measure. Disabled audiences have unfortunately become familiar with a collection of tired and harmful tropes, one of which is serving as “Inspiration Porn.” Series like A Perfect World center being disabled as nothing but constant misery, with their disabled characters only there to make those around them realize how much easier their own life is in comparison. The experiment lives at cdn.jamesst.one, which now serves a copy of this site, and you can watch where it is routing at rum.jamesst.one.

The above diagram is actually a simplification, because before that, a client first has to look up the IP address to connect to, i.e. DNS. A multi-CDN hooks into the DNS reply and picks which CDN is best, then that CDN’s anycast picks which specific data center based on network routing rules.

The CDN is chosen in DNS. When your resolver asks for cdn.jamesst.one, the answer is a CNAME to one of three CDNs, and which one depends on where you are. Or, more accurately, the network you are on.

The first version used a small script on the page that read Resource Timing entries and beaconed them home. Which works but I would rather not put JS on pages for this. jsDelivr itself gets its RUM data from elsewhere: I think it used Cedexis, then PerfOps, rather than running a script of its own.

items.title: Let's Play with Hardcaml!
items.label: Small Web
items.excerpt:
I prepared a five-minute lightning talk for the 8th Homebrew CPU Meetup on November 28, 2026. The slides are below.

Open slides in a new tab · Download PDF · View Markdown source

This talk is a gentle introduction to Hardcaml, an RTL design library embedded in OCaml. Rather than discussing advanced verification techniques, I wanted to share the fun of building digital circuits in an interactive programming environment.

We start with a simple 5-bit counter and do everything inside utop, an OCaml REPL:

No FPGA, external Verilog simulator, or even a separate OCaml project is needed to try this example. I tested the installation steps and the REPL session in a Docker environment, so you can follow along with the slides.

With the help of AI coding agents, I ended up building a dual-core RISC-V SoC that boots Linux 6.18 with SMP on a Colorlight i9 FPGA board.

I hope this talk encourages more people to give Hardcaml a try and enjoy building their own digital circuits.

items.title: Going by; Laughing; Living.
items.label: Small Web
items.excerpt:
Do you hear all this noise? It's frightening.

The sky is pink, and orange, and yellow all washed-out by the grey of the clouds.

A group of people is going by, they are laughing, they are living.

And I wonder how.

I'm trying to understand, how can I go by? How can I laugh? How can I live?

Why aren't they walking alone?

The room is getting dark, the colors have faded.

I can't hear the people anymore, but they are still walking around my brain.

They are going by, they are laughing, they are living.

Getting my head through the window, I am looking at the trees. Looking right in their eyes.

"I'm sorry", I tell them.

You didn't deserve this.

"You are precious", I tell them.

And I wonder why I don't hear it coming from everywhere.

Why is there only this scary noise?

The noise of life going on, of people going by.

As if it was all ok. As if all around us wasn't screaming.

But the noise is too loud, too loud to listen with our ears.

items.title: Mailwidget
items.label: Showcase
items.excerpt:
There's a MacOS app called TerminalWidget that can put terminal output in desktop widgets (I'll bet you saw that coming). Mailwidget is a shell script for creating a TerminalWidget that shows the unread count in any Mail.app mailboxes you choose.

There's a fair amount of fiddly configuration involved in making this work right, which is documented in the linked post. I did this to scratch an itch: there used to be utilities that would apply additional unread-count badges to Mail.app's icon, but those are long gone, and I wanted some approximation of that back.

items.label: Gaming
items.excerpt:
You struck a deal with a dragon: twenty years of protection for twenty years of dinner service. The island thrives under the beast's watchful eye, as long as the meals keep coming.

Every year, the dragon wakes up hungrier. You roll dice to work your island, harvest ingredients, fuse them into recipes, and cook them down in the Scorchpot — the pot you keep full or end up in. Get the meal right and you prosper. Get it wrong and you're smoke.

Build farmsteads, shrines, and harbors across your hex-grid island, each one changing how the board pays out. The best runs start with a handful of tiles and end with a machine that buries the dragon in food. Then the odds tighten, the dragon turns picky, and you tear the whole thing down and rebuild while it's on fire.

Feed the Scorchpot, keep the dragon happy, and outlast the contract.
